title: Windows Event Logs Cleared
exclusions: Detects Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog event 1102 recorded in the Security channel when the Security audit log is cleared and event 104 recorded in the System channel when Windows reports a named event-log channel was cleared. It does not prove which utility or process requested the clear, recover records removed by the operation, show whether an optional backup is complete, or establish malicious intent. Event 104's payload `Channel` names the cleared log; the event itself is still recorded in the System channel, so source channel and cleared channel must not be conflated. Event 1102 identifies the clearing account, domain, SID, and logon ID; event 104 does not provide the same SID/logon-ID contract. Circular overwrite, retention-based rollover, event-log service shutdown, disabled collection, deleted EVTX files that produce neither event, remote SIEM deletion, Linux logging, and cloud audit-log clearing are outside scope. Suppression changes notification only and must never discard the raw clear event.
evidence: After deployment, retain the effective `[WinEventLog://Security]` and `[WinEventLog://System]` inputs, installed add-on/forwarder versions, source-health and inventory reports, and the version-controlled `windows_event_log_cleared_1102_104` saved-search definition, ACL, schedule, dispatch history, triggered actions, and exported result rows. For every finding preserve the original XML event, `_time`, `_indextime`, recording host, recording channel, cleared log, event code, provider, subject name/domain/SID/logon ID when supplied, backup path when supplied, source, sourcetype, and EventRecordID, plus correlated logon/process/change records, investigation disposition, and any bounded notification exception. The clear event proves that Windows reported a clear operation; it does not preserve the removed records or prove the actor's motive. This documentation-only review created no Windows, Splunk, alert, recovery, or production evidence.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index and absolute time range, ingest two XML-rendered records from provider `Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog`: (a) `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, `EventCode=1102`, `Computer=WIN-DC01`, `SubjectUserName=clear_test`, `SubjectDomainName=CONTOSO`, `SubjectUserSid=S-1-5-21-111-222-333-1108`, `SubjectLogonId=0x12ab`, and `EventRecordID=910026`; and (b) `source=XmlWinEventLog:System`, the same sourcetype, `EventCode=104`, `Computer=WIN-APP01`, `SubjectUserName=SYSTEM`, `SubjectDomainName=NT AUTHORITY`, `Channel=Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational`, empty `BackupPath`, and `EventRecordID=910027`. Run a test copy with only the index changed. Expect exactly two rows: the 1102 row has `recording_channel=Security`, `cleared_log=Security`, and the SID/logon ID; the 104 row has `recording_channel=System`, `cleared_log=Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational`, and no fabricated SID/logon ID.
controlTest.negativeScenario: In a separate isolated interval, ingest (a) EventCode 1102 under `source=XmlWinEventLog:System`, (b) EventCode 104 under `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security`, (c) correctly sourced 1102 and 104 records from provider `Unrelated-Test-Provider`, and (d) correctly sourced provider events 1100 and 105. Expect zero rows because event/source/provider pairs are part of the contract and nearby event IDs are not log-clear records. Separately replay a valid System 104 with the cleared-log payload absent and confirm that the base report retains one row with `cleared_log=UNKNOWN`; a downstream notification may route incomplete telemetry for review but must not silently drop it.

dataSources: Primary sources are native Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog records collected continuously from each in-scope Windows host with the Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742): Security-channel event 1102 through `[WinEventLog://Security]` and System-channel event 104 through `[WinEventLog://System]`. The qualified XML contract is deployment-local `index=wineventlog`, `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog`, with `source=XmlWinEventLog:Security` or `source=XmlWinEventLog:System`. Event 1102 fields are `SubjectUserSid`, `SubjectUserName`, `SubjectDomainName`, `SubjectLogonId`, `Computer`, and `EventRecordID`; Event 104 fields are `SubjectUserName`, `SubjectDomainName`, payload `Channel` (the cleared log), `BackupPath`, `Computer`, and `EventRecordID`. Both require provider `Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog`, Splunk `_time`, `_indextime`, `host`, `source`, and `sourcetype`. Collection is event-driven Windows Event Log monitoring, not an API, HEC, scripted, or modular-input poll.
app: Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742), version 8.1.2 or a later platform-compatible release whose XML source/source-type and 1102/104 extraction contracts have been regression-tested locally. Splunkbase listed 10.0.1 as current on 2026-07-28 and compatible with Splunk 9.3/9.4 and 10.x; select a vendor-supported release for the deployed Splunk platform rather than assuming the newest package supports older releases. Deploy input configuration to Windows collection forwarders and the add-on's parsing/search-time knowledge to the required Splunk tiers. No premium app is required.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog" ((source="XmlWinEventLog:Security" EventCode=1102) OR (source="XmlWinEventLog:System" EventCode=104))
| eval event_code=tonumber(coalesce(EventCode,EventID,event_id)), provider_name=coalesce(Provider_Name,ProviderName,SourceName), recording_host=coalesce(Computer,ComputerName,dest,host), event_record_id=coalesce(EventRecordID,RecordNumber)
| eval provider_verified=if(lower(provider_name)="microsoft-windows-eventlog" OR match(_raw,"(?i)<Provider Name=['\"]Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog['\"]"),1,0)
| where provider_verified=1
| eval provider_name=coalesce(provider_name,"Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog"), recording_channel=if(event_code=1102,"Security","System"), payload_channel=mvindex(Channel,-1), cleared_log=case(event_code=1102,"Security",event_code=104 AND isnotnull(object) AND len(trim(object))>0,object,event_code=104 AND isnotnull(payload_channel) AND len(trim(payload_channel))>0,payload_channel,true(),"UNKNOWN")
| eval actor=coalesce(SubjectUserName,src_user,user,"UNKNOWN"), actor_domain=coalesce(SubjectDomainName,"UNKNOWN"), actor_sid=if(event_code=1102,SubjectUserSid,null()), actor_logon_id=if(event_code=1102,SubjectLogonId,null()), backup_path=if(event_code=104,coalesce(BackupPath,""),null()), input_source=source, use_case="UC-1.2.26"
| table _time _indextime recording_host recording_channel cleared_log event_code provider_name actor actor_domain actor_sid actor_logon_id backup_path event_record_id input_source sourcetype use_case
| sort 0 - _time
description: Reports each qualified Windows event-log clear operation observed as Security event 1102 or System event 104. It keeps the channel that recorded the event separate from the log that Windows says was cleared, preserves the event-specific actor fields without inventing a SID or logon ID for 104, and emits one evidence row per received clear record.
value: Clearing a Windows log can remove the local history needed for incident response, troubleshooting, and audit review. Immediate, semantics-correct reporting lets responders preserve remaining remote evidence and test whether an approved administrative or product workflow explains the operation, while avoiding false attribution caused by treating the System recording channel as the cleared log or assuming every clear is malicious.
implementation: Collect both local Security and System channels in XML with the Microsoft Windows add-on, qualify the provider and event-specific field shapes, and save the SPL as `windows_event_log_cleared_1102_104`. Schedule it every five minutes over a delayed, nonoverlapping five-minute window; trigger on any row, route Security 1102 and high-value cleared channels urgently, and retain all raw events. Apply only exact, expiring notification exceptions after detection, and require responders to corroborate the actor, logon, process, change, backup, and source-health context before declaring malicious log destruction.
visualization: Place a source-health row first for expected hosts missing Security or System telemetry, late events, parser failures, and duplicate EventRecordIDs. Below it show a newest-first clear-event table with recording host/channel, cleared log, event code, actor/domain/SID/logon ID, backup path, event record ID, source, and raw-event drilldown. Add a 24-hour timeline split by cleared log and event code, 30-day bars by actor and host, and a panel for `cleared_log=UNKNOWN`. Never use a green zero-count tile as proof that logs were not cleared; collection failure can also produce zero.
schema: Native Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog event 1102 and 104 XML contracts
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable to the authoritative rule. Current Windows add-on documentation does not provide one accelerated CIM dataset that guarantees both the raw 1102 Security event and 104 System event, the payload cleared-channel value, event-specific subject fields, backup path, provider, source channel, and EventRecordID. The previous generic `Change.All_Changes` search could return unrelated changes and could not prove these exact event pairs. Use the raw search for detection and evidence; build a summary only if it preserves the complete output contract and passes raw-event parity tests.

knownFalsePositives:
A qualifying 1102 or 104 is evidence that Windows reported a log clear; it is not a false event because the clear was authorized. A false positive occurs when downstream logic labels every clear malicious or pages without considering the cleared channel and actor context.

1. **Event Viewer or `wevtutil cl` used under an approved troubleshooting/change ticket** — Windows or application administrators may export and clear a corrupt, oversized, or test log. Match the exact host, cleared channel, named operator/service identity, ticket, optional backup path/hash, and bounded UTC window. Suppress notification only for that exact tuple and retain the event and exported evidence.

2. **Microsoft Exchange Managed Availability clearing a product-specific operational channel as `NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM`** — Exchange health workflows can produce System event 104 for channels such as `Microsoft-Exchange-ManagedAvailability/ThrottlingConfig`. Confirm the exact Exchange role/version, channel, SYSTEM subject, recurring cadence, and Microsoft/support-approved behavior on that host. Use a channel-and-host-specific expiring exception; never allow-list all SYSTEM clears or all Exchange servers.

3. **Golden-image, disposable-lab, automated test, or rebuild workflow** — Image-sealing or reset scripts may intentionally clear logs before handoff. Verify the CI/image job identity, ephemeral asset classification, build ID, and start/end time. Route to build evidence or suppress only those asset IDs during the job; a production host or off-schedule clear remains urgent.

4. **Backup-and-clear or archive rotation explicitly implemented by a legacy operations script** — A script using Event Viewer, PowerShell, WMI, or Windows event-log APIs can back up and then clear a channel. Require the script hash, scheduler/service identity, successful backup artifact, destination, retention check, and change owner. Suppress only after backup success is independently confirmed; `BackupPath` being nonempty does not prove a usable archive.

5. **Application vendor support procedure for a private Admin/Operational channel** — A vendor may direct support staff to clear one component channel after collecting diagnostics. Match the support case, exact channel, host, operator, and procedure; do not extend the exception to Security, System, Application, PowerShell, Defender, or EDR channels.

6. **Purple-team, red-team, incident-response drill, or control validation** — Approved tests intentionally invoke `wevtutil`, `Clear-EventLog`, or the Event Viewer UI. Require named testers, exact hosts/channels, exercise ID, and bounded time. Keep the base event visible and preserve the positive-control result; suppress only external paging if the exercise plan requires it.

7. **Unexpected `SYSTEM`, blank actor, or `cleared_log=UNKNOWN`** — These are incomplete or service-context telemetry, not benign classifications. Correlate Task Scheduler, Service Control Manager, Exchange/application, process-creation 4688/EDR, and change records. Never suppress solely because the subject is SYSTEM or a field is absent.

**Safe suppression:** keep `windows_event_log_cleared_1102_104` unsuppressed. A downstream `windows_event_log_clear_exceptions.csv` should require exact `recording_host,cleared_log,event_code,actor,rule_id`, owner, ticket, reason, numeric `valid_from_epoch`, and finite `valid_until_epoch`. Reject wildcards, host-wide or actor-wide entries, open-ended dates, and exceptions covering Security unless separately approved. Continue exporting suppressed matches and review exceptions at expiry.
reviewer: documentation-only editorial review against primary Microsoft event 1102 and archived event 104/provider semantics, Microsoft Windows event XML representation, Splunk Windows Event Log collection and add-on source/source-type documentation, Splunk Security Content, and MITRE ATT&CK; no Windows clear operation, fixture replay, add-on deployment, SPL execution, alert, recovery, production validation, Microsoft/Splunk SME review, or security sign-off

cost.search_load_notes: Sparse 1102/104 records are searched every five minutes over two already-collected Windows channels with exact source, event-code, and provider constraints. License and storage cost belongs primarily to the broader Security and System channel collection.

detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and exact event boundary

Assign Windows logging, endpoint security, Splunk data, detection-content, incident-response, and evidence owners. Inventory every in-scope Windows server and endpoint and decide whether direct local collection or Windows Event Forwarding owns each channel. The implementation must preserve the originating computer, source channel, event provider, event code, payload, event record ID, and event/index times. A WEC host must not replace the original computer with the collector identity.

Install a platform-compatible Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (`Splunk_TA_windows`, Splunkbase 742) and qualify the exact add-on, forwarder, Windows, and search-platform combination. Version 8.1.2 documents the XML source/source-type behavior used as a minimum content contract; Splunkbase listed 10.0.1 as current at review time but with a newer platform floor. No `splunkVersions` claim is made because this review did not execute a runtime matrix. The search role needs read and schedule permission for `index=wineventlog`; responders need raw-event access appropriate to sensitive usernames, domains, SIDs, hostnames, and logon identifiers. Neither the search nor alert action needs permission to clear logs, administer Windows, write exceptions, or delete evidence.

Understand the two records before deployment. Microsoft documents 1102 as generated whenever the Windows Security audit log is cleared. It is written in the Security channel by `Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog` and supplies `SubjectUserSid`, `SubjectUserName`, `SubjectDomainName`, and `SubjectLogonId`; that logon ID can be correlated with a nearby successful logon. Event 104 is written by the same provider in the System channel and its payload names the cleared channel and optional backup path. Therefore `source=XmlWinEventLog:System` is the place where 104 was recorded, not proof that the System log itself was the target. Do not invent a SID or logon ID for 104, and do not describe circular overwrite at maximum size as a clear operation.

The `wineventlog` index, saved-search name, schedule, delay, exception lookup, and retention are deployment-owned contracts rather than Microsoft or Splunk defaults. Change them consistently in inputs, SPL, controls, dashboards, evidence, and runbooks.

## Step 1 — Configure and qualify Security and System collection

Place local input settings in a deployment app or `Splunk_TA_windows/local/inputs.conf`; never edit the add-on's `default` directory. A representative direct-forwarder configuration is:

```ini
[WinEventLog://Security]
disabled = 0
start_from = oldest
current_only = 0
checkpointInterval = 5
renderXml = true
index = wineventlog

[WinEventLog://System]
disabled = 0
start_from = oldest
current_only = 0
checkpointInterval = 5
renderXml = true
index = wineventlog
```

Splunk documents XML as the default rendering mode from add-on 6.0.0 onward. The qualified contract here uses generic `sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog` and channel-specific sources `XmlWinEventLog:Security` and `XmlWinEventLog:System`. Classic rendering uses different source/source-type shapes and field aliases; do not claim `WinEventLog:Security` or `WinEventLog:System` is the source type for current XML data. If Classic is retained, write and fixture-test a separate compatibility search before changing this UC.

Windows Event Log monitoring is event-driven. There is no poll interval and no API response count: each published record collected after the checkpoint becomes an indexed event. Expected 1102/104 volume is normally sparse, while license volume is determined by all collected Security and System records. Measure daily bytes and indexing delay on representative domain controllers, member servers, application servers, and endpoints. Preserve enough local channel capacity to survive the longest forwarding outage; a record overwritten before forwarding cannot be reconstructed by Splunk.

Verify effective settings with `splunk btool inputs list WinEventLog://Security --debug` and the equivalent System stanza. After deployment, run a broad source-health query over at least 15 active minutes and require every expected host to report both qualified sources or an explicitly documented topology exception. Inspect one real or sanitized 1102 and 104 in raw XML. Confirm provider, EventCode, Computer, EventRecordID, subject fields, payload Channel, and BackupPath. Because 104 payload and System metadata can both contain a channel concept, confirm whether the installed add-on exposes the cleared target as `Channel`, `object`, or both; the SPL prefers normalized `object` and otherwise takes the last `Channel` value. Lock that behavior with fixtures.

Do not narrow inputs to only 1102/104 without a separate logging design review. Security and System context—including 4624, 4688, service, scheduler, event-log-service, and application records—supports investigation. If XML allow/deny filters are mandatory, use Splunk's documented `$XmlRegex` mechanism and test both event pairs, all context required by adjacent controls, checkpoint recovery, and upgrade behavior.

## Step 2 — Create, understand, schedule, and route the search

Save the catalogue SPL as `windows_event_log_cleared_1102_104`. Schedule it at `*/5 * * * *` with a closed delayed window such as `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`; keep time bounds in saved-search configuration rather than duplicating them in the portable catalogue SPL. Measure p95/p99 `_indextime-_time`; if ordinary delay exceeds five minutes, move the closed window or implement a tested late-arrival recovery search keyed by host, source, and EventRecordID.

### Understanding this SPL

The base search accepts only XML data and the two valid source/event pairs. This prevents a System 1102 or Security 104 fixture from being treated as equivalent. Numeric event normalization handles extracted EventCode variants, and provider filtering requires `Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog`, avoiding same-number records from unrelated providers. `recording_host` identifies the computer that wrote the event. `recording_channel` is derived from the qualified pair. For 1102, `cleared_log` is unambiguously Security. For 104, the search uses the add-on's normalized `object` when present and otherwise the payload channel extraction; missing target data remains `UNKNOWN` instead of disappearing.

Actor handling is event-specific. Both records can supply subject name/domain, but only 1102 is allowed to populate `actor_sid` and `actor_logon_id` under this contract. `backup_path` belongs only to 104 and is not interpreted as proof that a valid backup exists. EventRecordID, source, sourcetype, provider, event/index time, and the use-case ID remain in every output for evidence and drilldown. There is no count threshold: one qualified event is one finding.

Route 1102 and clears of Security, System, Application, PowerShell, Defender, EDR, authentication, and other high-value channels to urgent security review. Product-private operational-channel clears can use owner-specific severity only after baselining. Throttle exact host/cleared-log/actor combinations briefly while retaining every result. Never throttle by actor alone, especially SYSTEM, because it can hide a second host or channel. Do not automatically isolate a host, disable an account, stop EventLog, or restore an EVTX file from this event alone.

Keep the base report unsuppressed. Apply `windows_event_log_clear_exceptions.csv` only in a downstream notification search and require exact host, cleared log, event code, actor, rule ID, owner, ticket, reason, and finite epochs. Preserve exception match/revision in routed evidence. Unknown target or actor values must remain reviewable and cannot match wildcard exceptions.

## Step 3 — Validate source, semantics, controls, and completeness

Run both `controlTest` scenarios in an isolated index with absolute times. Assert two positive rows and every value, not merely a nonzero count. The 1102 fixture must remain Security/Security and retain SID/logon ID. The 104 fixture must remain System recording channel with the named PowerShell Operational log as the clear target and null SID/logon ID. Swapped sources, wrong providers, and adjacent IDs must return zero. The valid 104 missing target must return `UNKNOWN`, proving that incomplete evidence is surfaced rather than discarded.

For a safe live validation, use a disposable Windows lab host and a nonproduction channel. Export required records first, obtain Windows/security-owner approval, clear only the approved lab log through Event Viewer or `wevtutil cl`, and compare **Event Viewer > Windows Logs > Security** for 1102 and **Event Viewer > Windows Logs > System** for 104 with the Splunk result. Match UTC time, provider, recording computer, event ID, EventRecordID, subject, clear target, and backup path. Do not clear a production Security, System, application, EDR, or compliance log to test this control.

Compare bounded counts from Event Viewer or `Get-WinEvent` with Splunk on at least two representative hosts, allowing only measured pipeline latency. Test duplicate collection through WEF plus local input, checkpoint restart, delayed indexing, host rename/reimage, XML parsing after add-on upgrade, multivalue Channel extraction, absent BackupPath, unresolved SID, local and domain actors, and SYSTEM service context. Duplicate EventRecordIDs should become source-health findings; do not hide collection defects with broad `dedup`.

Maintain source health independently. Reconcile the expected-host inventory with recent Security and System event volume, forwarder phone-home, queues, and local channel state. Run `index=wineventlog sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog source IN ("XmlWinEventLog:Security","XmlWinEventLog:System") | timechart span=15m count by source limit=0` over 24 hours, but evaluate per-host gaps using a broader source-health rule. Zero clear events is normal; zero source telemetry is not evidence that no clear occurred.

## Step 4 — Operationalize investigation, dashboard, and evidence

Build the dashboard described in `visualization` with source health first. Restrict exception writes and raw Security data to the appropriate roles. A general operations view can show host, cleared log, time, event code, and case state; the security view can expose subject identifiers, backup path, correlated logons/processes, raw XML, and asset criticality. Label recording channel, cleared log, and recording host explicitly.

The response runbook should: (1) verify the raw provider/event/source pair and event identity; (2) identify the exact cleared log and whether target data is missing; (3) determine whether the subject is a user, service, SYSTEM, unresolved SID, or unavailable; (4) correlate 1102's SubjectLogonId with nearby 4624 and process-creation/EDR telemetry for Event Viewer, `wevtutil.exe`, PowerShell, WMI, or application service activity; (5) review scheduler, service, Exchange/application, image, support, test, and change records; (6) verify any claimed backup independently and preserve its hash/access controls; (7) check forwarding and local retention for evidence loss; (8) assess whether other hosts/channels were cleared; and (9) record disposition, scope, containment, and recovery.

Treat MITRE ATT&CK T1070.001 as an investigative hypothesis. Confirmed adversarial clearing supports that technique; an approved support operation or automated product maintenance does not become malicious merely because the same event fired. Conversely, SYSTEM is not automatically benign. Escalate when high-value channels, multiple hosts, suspicious logons/processes, defense impairment, or gaps coincide.

Retain the artifacts named in `evidence` under the local incident and audit policy. The cost profile's 90-day value is advisory planning metadata, not a legal retention requirement. The 1102/104 records prove observed clear operations only; they do not prove continuous collection, reconstruct removed content, authenticate a backup, establish authorization, or satisfy a regulation by themselves.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot without weakening the rule

- **No event after an approved lab clear:** inspect Event Viewer first, confirm which log was cleared and where Windows wrote 1102 or 104, then verify both effective input stanzas, channel permission, checkpoint, forwarding queues, index route, and search time. Do not enable a broader event-ID-only rule to mask source failure.
- **Events arrive as `WinEventLog:Security` or channel-suffixed source types:** the deployment uses Classic or a historical contract. Inspect raw metadata and add-on version; migrate to XML or create a separately tested branch with its real fields. Do not label channel-specific values as current XML sourcetypes.
- **Provider is null:** ensure XML is intact and the add-on's parsing/search-time knowledge is deployed to the required tier. Compare `_raw` and effective props. Qualify a precise extraction from the XML Provider element rather than removing provider validation.
- **104 says `recording_channel=System` but the dashboard claims System was cleared:** the dashboard is using source channel as target. Restore the `cleared_log` output from `object`/payload Channel and test a non-System target such as PowerShell Operational.
- **`cleared_log=UNKNOWN`:** inspect raw UserData and extraction/multivalue behavior. Keep the finding, fix parsing, and investigate the host; do not coalesce the source's System channel into the missing target.
- **1102 actor is wrong or absent:** inspect `SubjectUserName`, `SubjectUserSid`, `SubjectDomainName`, and `SubjectLogonId` in raw XML. Do not substitute host, recorder, or CIM `user` without field-level verification.
- **104 has no SID or logon ID:** expected under this documented event-specific contract. Correlate subject name/domain, process, scheduler, service, and other telemetry; never copy 1102-only fields into 104.
- **Duplicate clear rows:** compare recording computer, source, EventRecordID, `_raw`, and `_indextime`; check WEF plus local collection, cloned checkpoints, replay, and duplicate routes. Repair collection and preserve the duplicate finding.
- **Clear event appears authorized but no backup can be opened:** treat backup verification separately. A path or operator statement is not proof of completeness, integrity, retention, or access.
- **Alert volume from product-private channels:** baseline exact host/channel/actor workflows, validate with the application owner, and use bounded exact downstream exceptions. Never suppress all 104, all SYSTEM, or an entire host.
grandmaExplanation: We record when Windows says one of its event histories was cleared, which computer reported it, which history was affected, and who Windows named when that information is available. That helps the team protect remaining evidence and check whether the action was approved.
hardware: Supported Microsoft Windows Server and Windows client systems whose local Security and System event channels are collected through a qualified direct-forwarder or Windows Event Forwarding topology. Collector architectures must preserve the originating computer and event payload; the WEC host is transport infrastructure, not automatically the system whose log was cleared.
